title: Review (Avot 3:8)
hookLine: whoever lets learning slip away through neglect loses something precious
tomorrow: what happens if you do more than you know?

cards: Six weeks after the final, the formulas have quietly packed up and left. So how bad is it to forget what you learned?
Rabbi Dostai bar Yannai, quoting Rabbi Meir, sounds harsh in Avot: whoever forgets even one thing of his learning, Scripture counts it as if he put his life at risk.
Then, in the very same mishnah, the sages argue with that. Two views, one paragraph.

teach.h: THE STRICT VIEW: GUARD WHAT YOU WERE GIVEN.
teach.b: The strict view first, at its best. Rabbi Meir's verse is Deuteronomy: "Only take heed to thyself, and keep thy soul diligently, lest thou forget the things which thine eyes have seen."
Learning, on this view, is something you were trusted with, like a key or a child. Letting it slip is not a small thing, because what's forgotten can't be passed on.
The strict view protects what you love from slow neglect. Now the other view, and the Mishnah gives it itself. Could this apply even if the learning was too hard for him?
No: the same verse goes on, "and lest they depart from thy heart all the days of thy life." He isn't at fault until he sits and removes them from his heart.
Forgetting under pressure, or because the material was simply hard, isn't the failure.

teach.h: THE OTHER: ONLY TURNING AWAY COUNTS.
teach.b: Turning away from it is. That view protects the learner from despair.
Both agree on the cure, and the outline names it in one word: review.
The Talmud has a line for it: one who reviews his chapter a hundred times is not like one who reviews it a hundred and one times.
The extra pass is where it becomes yours.

how: Jews review what they've studied by going over a page again with a study partner or at a class, and some keep a daily cycle of learning that returns to the same texts.

o: going over learning again so it doesn't slip away
a judge's look back at a case already decided
a test given at the end of a year of study

games.q: two views on forgetting — tap the pairs.
p: lest they depart from thy heart

s: Avot says anyone who forgets anything is guilty, no matter what
the same mishnah says not if the learning was too hard; only if he removes it from his heart.
the Talmud says reviewing a hundred and one times beats a hundred
the extra pass is the point.
Rabbi Meir's harsh line comes with a verse from Deuteronomy
take heed to thyself… lest thou forget.

games.q: your friend says Avot 3:8 is too harsh: who hasn't forgotten things? what's the best case for the strict reading?
o: it guards what you were trusted with from slow neglect.
it proves memory is the only thing that really counts.
it means anyone who forgets is beyond help.
games.why: the strict view treats learning as a trust, to be passed on. the same mishnah softens it: the fault is turning away, not struggling.

practice: Say out loud one thing you learned this year, a line, a fact, a skill, in a single sentence. Then say it again, a little slower: the hundred-and-first time. Let the second pass catch something the first one missed.

wordCard.voice: Review: Avot 3:8's quiet cure for forgetting. Go over it again, one more time than feels necessary.

orig.note: Hebrew: one who forgets one thing of his learning, Avot 3:8.

carryVoice: Keep this: review, once more than you think you need, and it stays yours. Same time tomorrow.
